endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: If it does not meet the 2053 requirements, an error message will be displayed.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Incomplete, ambiguous, or no result of the logistic regression model (AE risk score), resulting in a delay in AE risk score output, which then increases the wait time for clinician review and/or communication with the patient, and an error value indication (“unavailable”) is shown.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether an explicit error or unavailable indication keeps clinicians from reading a missing or invalid AI result as normal, and no study documents how often that misreading occurs. The recommendation currently rests on an FDA draft guidance and the CHAI assurance guide, both of which describe the practice rather than evaluate it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Both endorsements are descriptive examples within guidance documents. Under GRADE conventions no certainty rating can be assigned, and the effect on clinician interpretation or patient outcomes remains unmeasured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions gives an example in which an error message appears when inputs fail requirements. This suggests reviewers may expect manufacturers to describe such behavior in submissions. The guidance is a draft and uses the language of illustration, so it does not by itself establish a binding requirement for deployers.

The CHAI guide lists an incomplete or absent risk score as a failure mode that delays clinician review and patient communication, with an unavailable value shown. This framework identifies the failure pathway, but no supplied data show whether the indication shortens that delay or prevents a missing score from being read as low risk.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often clinicians misread blank, stale, or invalid AI outputs as normal findings, and that compare explicit error or unavailable displays against current interfaces for detection rates, time to clinician follow-up, and downstream patient events.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether error indications work equally well in understaffed settings, or for patient-facing tools used by people with limited English or literacy, is unknown.
